newsitem.title: USA: Dollar posts eight-week high versus mark, yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar posts eight-week high versus mark, yen.

text.p: The dollar extended Monday's gains to eight-week highs versus the mark and yen Tuesday, after a Federal Reserve official fuelled speculation that U.S. interest rates would soon rise.
The dollar worked its way above another key technical level at 1.51 marks, after Fed Governor Janet Yellen said on Tuesday the U.S. economy was in an "inflationary danger zone".

The dollar also derived strength from Monday's remarks by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke, who said German overnight lending rates could fall if money supply growth slows further and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who said central bankers of the G10 nations agreed a strong dollar was in everyone's interest.

"On a technical basis the dollar looks very solid and there's not any contrary fundamentals that would put a lot of fear into people these days," said Dan O'Connell, vice president at First Chicago NBD Bank.
Buying by traders who watch technical factors such as trends on price charts pushed the dollar to nearly 110 yen on Tuesday, as against the mark, its highest level since July 16.
On Tuesday, the dollar rose to 1.5110 marks up from 1.5003 late Monday and to 109.85 yen, up from 109.25 yen.
Yellen told Reuters she had been surprised by the robust 4.8 percent rate of econmic growth so far this year.
Her comments aided widespread market speculation that Fed policy makers are sufficiently worried about rekindled inflation that they will soon raise short-term interest rates.
Higher U.S. interest rates typically bolster the dollar by making deposits denominated in it more attractive. Similarly, lower German rates should weaken the mark.
But Yellen's remarks did not blindside the market, according to analysts.
The market has been pricing in a Fed credit tighting after several weeks of strong economic data, particulartly a drop in the August unemployment rate to 5.1 percent, from 5.4 percent.

"I guess the expectation is that we are looking at an interest rate hike of a quarter percent," said Tim Summerfield, senior foreign exchange trader at Bank of Boston. "The market is comfortable with it."

The Federal Reserve is expected to set the level of the key fed funds rate -- the rate banks charge each other for overnight borrowing -- at 5.5 percent from its current 5.25 percent when it meets on September 24.

The dollar broke above the key 1.50 mark barrier on Monday and some analysts attribute the dollar's continued gains to waves of speculators chasing the dollar higher, betting that a trend towards rising prices is in place.
"Yellen's remarks may have sparked a little fear but people already new that," said Mary Beth Slack, foreign exchange analyst at consulting firm MCM CurrencyWatch.
"What you are seeing here is largely a technical rally; we broke out two days ago and there has really been no looking back since then," she said.
Dealers bet that if they quickly buy after the dollar breaks above a technical threshold, they will be able to sell for a profit at an even higher price.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2355 Swiss francs from 1.2233 on Monday and to Canadian $1.3705 from C$1.3704.
